summary: Describes version 2 of the Session Announcement Protocol, a multicast session directory announcement protocol, along with security and scalability issues for implementors. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: SAP lets an announcer send session descriptions to multicast listeners within the same scope. Announcements repeat periodically, and the announcer does not know which listeners received them.

subtitle: How Session Announcement Protocol multicasts session descriptions and manages their updates and deletion.

tldr.problem: People need to discover multicast sessions and get the information required to join them, without an announcer tracking individual listeners.
tldr.mechanism: An announcer periodically multicasts a session description to the session's scope. Listeners receive the announcements, while optional authentication supports checks on changes and deletions.
tldr.outcome: SAP version 2 is an Experimental protocol for session announcements. It adds no reliability beyond best-effort UDP and is not designed for timely discovery.

today: RFC 2974 is an Experimental RFC published in October 2000, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes version 2 of the Session Announcement Protocol.

sections.title: Announcing Multicast Sessions
sections.content:
The Session Announcement Protocol (SAP) describes how a session directory advertises multicast sessions. An announcer periodically sends a packet containing a session description to a well-known multicast address and port. Listeners monitor the SAP address for the multicast scopes in which they participate.

There is no rendezvous mechanism: the announcer does not know whether listeners exist. SAP provides no extra reliability beyond best-effort UDP/IP. The announcement SHOULD contain an authentication header, and the description MAY be encrypted, though encryption is not recommended for groups with many receivers who cannot decrypt it.
sections.plainLanguage: An announcer periodically sends a session description to a multicast group. Listeners can receive it, but the announcer does not know whether any listener received it.

sections.title: Addresses, Scope and Announcement Rate
sections.content:
Announcements use the same multicast scope as the session. SAP packets MUST use port 9875 and SHOULD use an IP time-to-live of 255. For IPv4 global-scope sessions, announcements go to 224.2.127.254; administrative-scope announcements use the highest multicast address in the relevant zone. IPv6 announcements use FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:2:7FFE, with X set to the scope value.

Unless configured otherwise, the bandwidth limit SHOULD be 4000 bits per second per SAP group. The interval depends on the number and size of announcements and the configured limit; a random offset helps avoid synchronized transmissions. The announcer recalculates before transmission to reduce bursts after startup or a network partition heals.
sections.plainLanguage: An announcement goes only to the multicast scope of its session and uses a specified port. Announcers share a rate limit so the announcement traffic does not grow without control.

sections.title: SAP Header and Session Changes
sections.content:
The SAP header includes a version field, address type, reserved bit, message type, encryption and compression bits, authentication length, message identifier hash, and originating source. The version value MUST be 1. A message type distinguishes an announcement from a deletion. Compression uses zlib, and when both compression and encryption are used, compression MUST happen first.

The message identifier hash and source identify an announcement version. Announcers SHOULD NOT set either field to zero. A payload type identifies the content format; every implementation MUST support application/sdp. To modify a session, an announcer changes the identifier hash and must satisfy the authentication or source rules for modifying the cached announcement. Deletion can use an explicit deletion packet or a timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the source and version of an announcement and says whether it is a new session or a deletion. Changes must be distinguishable from earlier announcements and follow the authentication rules.

sections.title: Authentication, Encryption and Risks
sections.content:
The authentication header can verify that a change or deletion is permitted and can help authenticate the session creator. Its digital signature covers the entire packet, including the header. The RFC describes PGP and CMS authentication formats but does not require one authentication mechanism.

The RFC does not specify the encryption algorithm or how keys are generated and distributed. Encrypted announcements are NOT RECOMMENDED for broad groups where many listeners cannot decrypt them. Authentication rules also help prevent a forged announcement from being treated as a valid modification or deletion. A denial-of-service attack based on flooding a nearby announcer is described, and the RFC supplies no mechanism to prevent it.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature can help listeners check that a session change came from an authorized source. Encryption is only useful when listeners have the key, and the RFC leaves encryption and key distribution details unspecified.

sections.title: Caching and Discovery Delay
sections.content:
SAP is intended for long-lived, wide-area multicast sessions and repeats announcements on the order of tens of minutes. A new listener may therefore wait a long time to learn all sessions. The protocol is not especially timely.

The RFC recommends proxy caches to reduce this delay. A proxy listens to SAP groups in its scope and keeps an updated list of sessions and the time each announcement was last received. The protocol for a listener to contact its local proxy is not specified.
sections.plainLanguage: A listener may wait for the next repeated announcement before learning about a session. A proxy can provide a cached list sooner, but this RFC does not specify how listeners contact that proxy.

viz.caption: THE FIRST 32 BITS OF THE SAP HEADER

fields.name: A
fields.desc: Address type: 0 for IPv4, 1 for IPv6.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: Indicates whether the payload is encrypted.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Indicates whether the payload is compressed.

fields.name: Auth length
fields.desc: Number of 32-bit words of authentication data.

fields.name: Message ID hash
fields.desc: Identifies the announcement version with the originating source.
